articles.title: The Verge Awards at CES 2026
articles.summary: Rollable laptops, twice-folding phones, and a ‘longevity station.’ This is the CES tech that deserves an award.
articles.body: Every January, the world of consumer electronics heads to Las Vegas to spend the first full week of the year in the desert presenting, prodding, and gawking at all the new gadgets and gear debuting at CES. The show has once again delivered an avalanche of products, both innovative and vaporous, that will shape the industry in 2026. The Verge’s team has been working around the clock to share the experience. Some of it wowed us while some of it weirded us out, but that’s part of the fun of CES. After taking it all in over the past week, there are some gadgets that stood out from the rest. They innovated on an existing product, entirely rethought a category, or delivered something so delightful or dumb that we just had to share. These are the things that deserve to be recognized — our best of CES 2026. In this article Best monitor LG Display’s 27-inch 4K RGB-stripe OLED panel [Image: Samsung screens have dominated The Verge Awards at CES four years in a row, but it’s LG Display’s time to shine again. Both companies have finally managed to produce gorgeous high-refresh-rate OLED panels whose pixels contain the proper number of linearly repeating red, green, and blue components to clearly render text — addressing the annoying color fringing that can sometimes make text hard to read on previous-gen OLED screens. But after looking at LG Display’s and Samsung Display’s screens in back-to-back appointments, Verge display expert John Higgins and I had to give LG Display the edge. With 4K resolution at 27 inches, text and gaming graphics were both incredibly sharp and easy on the eyes. It’s also a dual-mode 4K 240Hz or 1080p 480Hz panel, so you can switch to an even higher refresh rate. It’s not the brightest or highest-resolution screen we saw at CES, where brilliant 5K 1,500-nit monitors were also on display — this one has 1,000-nit peaks — but it’s the one I’d pick for work and play. Asus might be one of the first to use it in the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM, which’ll have DisplayPort 2.1a, HDMI 2.1, and a 90W USB-C port so you can dock and charge a laptop, but it didn’t share price or availability. — Sean Hollister, senior editor Best keyboard Corsair’s Galleon 100 SD [Image: There are always a lot of cool keyboards at CES. This year might be one of the best, if only because among all of the new, interesting models was Corsair’s $350 Galleon 100 SD that’ll be available later this month. It’s a full-size wired mechanical keyboard that just so happens to have a Stream Deck built in. Its greatest feat is that it manages to not look like a botched experiment. While part of the Stream Deck’s appeal comes from the fact that it’s typically sold as a peripheral, set off to the side on your desk where you can easily reach it to mute your mic, launch an app, or configure your smart lights, it looks and feels right at home fused into this keyboard. This particular hardware is closest to a Stream Deck Plus, with a screen, two rotary knobs, and 12 buttons, each of which can be customized however you’d like via Elgato’s vast marketplace of app plug-ins, icons, sounds, and more. The Galleon looks cutting-edge, although the keyboard aspect doesn’t necessarily stand out compared to many models already available. It has Corsair’s own mechanical switches, a hot-swappable PCB, up to 8,000Hz polling rate, and it can be configured in the company’s browser-based utility, negating the need for a software download. I’m actually using the Galleon to type this, and I don’t have much to complain about so far. — Cameron Faulkner, commerce editor Best TV TCL X11L SQD-Mini LED [Image: TCL made a bold move for CES 2026. Instead of focusing mainly on RGB LEDs like its competitors, it instead went all in on its new X11L SQD-Mini LED TV, which uses blue LEDs like the mini-LED TVs we’re familiar with. But there are two major improvements TCL made that set it apart, and that you won’t find on any other TV this year. The X11L uses reformulated quantum dots that provide more color and an upgraded color filter TCL calls UltraColor Filter that delivers more accurate color. The two combine to cover 100 percent of the BT.2020 color space. It’s an innovation that I expect will eventually filter into other, more affordable models — both from TCL and other manufacturers. In addition to the vibrant colors, the X11L is capable of reaching 10,000 nits of peak brightness and has up to 20,000 dimming zones. The innovation doesn’t come cheap, with the smallest X11L at 75 inches going for $6,999.99, but by the end of the year, it will very possibly be almost half that price. — John Higgins, senior TVs and audio reviewer Best laptop Asus ROG Zephyrus Duo [Media: Asus is back for round two with its ROG Zephyrus Duo dual-screen gaming laptop, and I think this one could be a real knockout. The new Duo has two matching edge-to-edge 16-inch OLED displays, up to RTX 5090 graphics, an Intel Panther Lake processor, and a removable wireless keyboard / trackpad deck. It’s a clamshell laptop, a top-and-bottom or side-by-side multiscreen setup, and even a tented convertible all-in-one machine. Dual-screen laptops are nerdy fun, but I’ve seen firsthand how handy they are for productivity in my time testing the Lenovo Yoga Book 9i. Taking that power-user formula to a gaming laptop seems like a recipe for success in my book. We sadly still don’t know the price of the new Zephyrus Duo — just that it’s due out in Q2 2026. Dual-screen laptops will always be a pricier niche, and I’m afraid it’s gonna be really up there; especially with two large OLEDs and the ongoing RAM shortage. Here’s to hoping the premium over the Zephyrus G16 it’s based on isn’t astronomical, because it looks awesome. I can’t wait to review it and see how I can simultaneously mix work and play on its lovely dual displays. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer Best smart home device Aqara Smart Lock U400 [Image: Smart locks were once again the smart home stars of the show, with companies launching models featuring palm- and facial-recognition unlocking, as well as a new type of wireless charging. But the standout was the Aqara Smart Lock U400 — not because of any particular innovation on Aqara’s part. It’s a fairly standard-looking smart lock. Rather, it represents how open standards, interoperability, and some genuinely cool technology are making the smart home smarter and easier to use. The first smart lock to support Apple’s hands-free Home Key unlocking using ultra-wideband technology, the U400 can securely unlock as you approach with your phone in your pocket or your Apple Watch on your wrist. As a Matter-over-Thread device, it can work with any Matter-compatible smart home platform, including Google Home, Amazon Alexa, Home Assistant, and Samsung SmartThings. While this magical hands-free unlocking experience (I tested the lock ahead of CES and it works very well) is currently limited to Apple, the U400 is Aliro-ready. Aliro is a smart lock standard developed by Apple, Samsung, Google, and lock and chip makers that will bring Home Key-style hands-free unlocking — along with NFC tap-to-unlock — to Android phones and watches. That’s a meaningful step toward solving the fragmentation and ecosystem lock-in that has long plagued the smart home. — Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, senior smart home reviewer Best car Mercedes Drive Assist Pro [Image: My pick for best car at CES was kind of a no-brainer, because it was the only thing real enough for us to test ourselves. That would be Mercedes’ Drive Assist Pro, which is a Level 2 partially autonomous driver assist feature for city driving as well as highways. The system is powered by five radar sensors, 10 cameras, and 12 ultrasonic sensors. And all that sensor data is shoveled into a supercomputer from Nvidia that is capable of running up to 508 trillion operations a second. I went on a test ride through San Francisco and was pretty impressed with how the system handled all the chaos of a crowded city. There were bike messengers, double-parked cars, delivery trucks, and people pushing baby strollers, and the Mercedes navigated all of it pretty effortlessly. It’s not a fully autonomous system yet, and the driver still needs to keep their eyes on the road and hands on the wheel. But you can see how those restrictions could eventually be lifted if Mercedes decides it’s safe enough to do so. Think of it as Mercedes’ answer to Tesla’s Full Self-Driving, but arguably a lot more robust thanks to all those extra sensors. In my opinion it beats Tesla’s camera-only approach just in terms of redundancy. Also it’s backed by Nvidia’s safety-certified silicon chips and AI software, all of which are going into a lot more cars in the years to come. — Andrew J. Hawkins, transportation editor Best health tech Withings Body Smart 2 [Image: This year’s show was all about longevity tech, and some pretty cursed ways to tackle that concept. Mostly involving several bodily fluids and inconvenient tests. The Withings Body Scan 2, however, is a scale, and everyone knows how to use a scale. The interesting thing: Withings is positioning this device less as a scale and more as a “longevity station.” It measures over 60 biomarkers, concentrating on cardiovascular and non-invasive metabolic health. It does the latter by measuring minuscule amounts of foot sweat. (And while technically foot sweat is a bodily fluid, I’ll take that over urine or blood.) More so than the fancy metrics, what I like here is the concept of decentering weight from the entire purpose of a scale. It’s encouraging users to view their weight as one part of their health — not the entire measure. My only gripe is that the scale will cost a whopping $600, but hopefully the price for this kind of tech comes down over time. — Victoria Song, senior reviewer Best wearable L’Oréal LED Face Mask [Image: This was a ho-hum year for wearables at the show, so I was pleasantly surprised by L’Oréal’s take on an LED face mask — a product category I generally hate. It’s conceptually based on a sheet mask, meaning it’s much easier to wear than the typical, Jason Voorhees-esque LED masks you’ll find on the show floor. It’s made of a flexible, silicone-esque material, and the light sits much closer to your skin. There’s also a smaller version that fits just under the eyes. The flexible material also means that, down the line, you could see this technology applied to other body parts, such as the neck or decolletage. Plus, you only have to wear it for five to 10 minutes. What I appreciate about this mask is that L’Oréal has disclosed it uses 630nm and 830nm wavelengths, and that it’s going through the extra hoops of 510(k) FDA clearance. No one needs red light therapy masks, and it’s totally fine if you don’t believe it’s a useful therapy. However, the combination of a smarter design, transparent labeling, and regulatory compliance is the type of innovation I want to see in a market that’s rampant with scammy versions of the same gadget. — Victoria Song, senior reviewer Best hair dryer/lamp Dreame Halo [Image: Do I need a giant hair dryer with LEDs? No. But would I use it? Absolutely. Drying my hair is one of my least favorite activities, and I would love to veg out on the couch or play games at my computer while Dreame’s $700 standing hair dryer does all the work for me. No one even has to know that you have a hair dryer in your living room or office, either; you can just turn on the light, and it becomes a lamp — albeit an excessive one. — Emma Roth, news writer Best gaming 8BitDo Ultimate 3E Controller for Xbox [Image: 8BitDo made a name for itself with affordable but well-featured alternatives to Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo’s often pricey controllers. The company is still very good at that, but with the new Ultimate 3E Controller for Xbox, 8BitDo demonstrates it can offer a better product than the console makers and compete with other high-end controller makers. When it launches in Q2 of 2026 for $149.99, the Ultimate 3E will be 8BitDo’s most expensive controller to date, but it delivers plenty of features to justify that price. It’s got drift-resistant tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) joysticks with reactive LED lighting at their base, Hall effect triggers with adjustable stops, two sets of shoulder buttons, motion controls, and four haptic feedback motors. It connects to recent Xbox consoles using an included 2.4GHz dongle, and other devices using Bluetooth or a USB-C cable. The Ultimate 3E is also extensively customizable. It works with 8BitDo’s Ultimate Software X so you can remap its controls and adjust the sensitivity of its triggers and sticks. You can swap out its standard joysticks with replacements that are taller or thicker, or upgrade its metal D-pad to one with a circular design. You can even change how the Ultimate 3E’s ABXY buttons feel. They’re all contained in interchangeable button modules featuring either squishy silicone membrane buttons or clicky micro switches. If it’s a premium Xbox controller you’re after, 8BitDo is now worth your consideration. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter Best phone Samsung Galaxy Z TriFold [Image: You know what’s better than a folding phone? A folding phone that folds again. Yes, it’s almost certainly going to be outrageously expensive. Yes, Huawei already did a trifold. And yes, it’s kind of nonsense to call it a trifold when it only folds twice. But gosh dang it, it’s so cool. Just to recap: The TriFold is on sale currently in Korea, and Samsung plans to sell it in the US later this year at a to-be-disclosed price. It folds up like a wallet, with a 6.5-inch outer screen for when you want it to be a phone and a massive 10-inch inner screen when you need a tablet. Mostly I’m just impressed that it’s really here. Samsung started hinting at its existence last January at Unpacked; just under a year later, it’s a reality that I was able to touch, hold, and flex. And it’s all the more appealing because, in true Samsung fashion, you can do whatever the hell you want with it. Particularly with the inner screen — it functions like an Android phone by default, but you can put it into DeX mode if you want a more PC-like experience with windowing. – Allison Johnson, senior reviewer Best audio product Fender Mix Headphones [Image: I’ve listened to a lot of headphones throughout my career, to the point where it sometimes feels like a chore. So when I put a pair on my head and immediately enjoy what I hear, I take notice. From the moment I put the Fender Mix headphones on my head, I knew I had found something special. The audio tuning sounded full without being overpowering. The ear cups were cushiony and the headphones had a strong amount of clamping force, but not so much that I got a headache, to keep them securely in place. And they felt well built and durable. But the best part about them are the details. By removing one of the ear cups, you can access a door that opens to allow you to change the rechargeable battery if it ever fails. The battery gets you 100 hours of listening time (52 with ANC). And under the other ear cup is a USB-C dongle you can plug into your device to allow it to transmit an Auracast broadcast to the headphones. The headphones support low-latency, lossless, and high-res audio at 24-bit/96kHz. And if your battery runs out, you can connect a cable to the 3.5mm port and listen to them passively. The short time I was able to spend with the Fender Mix headphones was one of the highlights of my CES. — John Higgins, senior TVs and audio reviewer Best robot Roborock’s Saros Rover [Image: It was the year of the robot at CES, with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas and LG’s CLOiD making their Las Vegas debuts alongside hundreds of humanoid bots hanging around every booth. But while some of these robots gave (somewhat) impressive demos and hinted at a more compelling narrative as to how they could one day be useful in our homes, it’s clear that the Rosie the Robot-style home helper is still firmly part of science fiction. Instead, the best robot at CES was the one that simply climbed the stairs and cleaned them. Robot vacuum maker Roborock debuted the Saros Rover, the world’s first robot vacuum that can both climb stairs and clean them. While we’ve seen concepts from Dreame and Eufy featuring track-equipped robots that can haul a vacuum upstairs to clean multiple floors, the Rover takes it a step further. With froglike legs on wheels, the Rover methodically tackled a flight of stairs in its CES debut, pivoting on one leg at each step as it vacuumed along the treads. The Rover is still a concept product with no price or release date, but stairs have been the final frontier for these popular home-cleaning robots — and it looks like Roborock just conquered them. — Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, senior smart home reviewer Best surprise HP Eliteboard G1a [Media: Surprise! This fairly thin, unassuming office keyboard from HP is actually a desktop computer. Inside is an AMD Ryzen AI 300-series processor, RAM, storage, a fan, stereo speakers, and mics — it’s the full package. It even comes with a pre-paired Bluetooth mouse and options for a user-replaceable battery and fingerprint reader embedded in the power button. You just need to plug into a monitor delivering power via USB-C. It’s surprisingly fun and quirky for a device designed for dull enterprise and IT duties. It feels like a throwback to the days of the legendary Commodore 64 with Raspberry Pi 500 DNA sprinkled in, though with a number pad and much more power. A laptop probably makes more sense for most people (even office workers), but the Eliteboard G1a is much more unique. It may not be as nice to type on as the mechanical keyboards I covet so much, but for a latticeless membrane board it ain’t bad. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer Best promise Donut Lab’s solid-state battery [Image: Donut Lab’s claim to have a solid-state battery ready to go into production raised more than just a few eyebrows at CES this year. After all, a battery that swaps liquid electrolytes for solid material would mean smaller, more energy-dense, more durable, longer-lasting, and less fire-prone batteries. In other words, a potential game changer in the world of electric vehicles. Of course, the landscape is littered with the corpses of companies promising solid-state breakthroughs, so Donut Lab needs to back its claims up with real proof. The company is promising production is imminent, so either way we should know soon enough. — Andrew J. Hawkins, transportation editor Best backpedal Dell bringing back XPS [Image: Last year, for the category of “Best new Dell computer name,” we awarded no winners because of Dell’s baffling decision to kill the XPS brand in favor of generic monikers like Dell, Dell Pro, and Dell Pro Max. This year, thankfully, Dell ate some humble pie and brought XPS back, even putting the XPS brand on the lid of the laptops. Dell Pro is still around, but we can deal with that now that XPS has returned. — Jay Peters, senior reporter Best use of E Ink SwitchBot Weather station [Image: There were more digital picture frames using E Ink’s advanced color e-paper screen tech debuting at CES this year, but SwitchBot finding an alternate use for the black-and-white E Ink panels typically found in e-readers impressed us more. As the name implies, the SwitchBot Weather Station focuses on providing a wealth of weather-related info for both inside and outside your home using built-in sensors and downloaded data. Its simplicity is its biggest appeal. It’s all displayed on a 7.5-inch E Ink monochromatic screen that’s wrapped in a basic black frame you can prop up on a table or hang on a wall. Pricing and availability aren’t known yet, but the Weather Station can also display calendar data synced from various platforms, and offers limited control of your smart home through the SwitchBot Hub. As with a lot of devices announced at CES 2026, the Weather Station has some AI-powered features, too, but they’re limited to offering weather-related insights and aspirational quotes that could help get you through a dreary day. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter Best thing we’d actually buy Ikea’s Kallsup Bluetooth speakers [Media: There’s no shortage of cheap Bluetooth speakers on the market — Amazon is flooded with them — but they’re always a gamble. Will they sound okay? Will their rechargeable battery be safe? Will their wireless connection be reliable? Last November Ikea introduced a new collection of colorful Bluetooth speakers that can double as home decor, but at CES it announced a much smaller alternative that’s priced to be an impulse purchase. The next time we stop by for meatballs and cheap bookshelves, we’re probably going to be walking out of an Ikea warehouse with an armful of its new Kallsup Bluetooth speakers. Available in white, pink, and lime green color options when it launches in April 2026, the Kallsup is a tiny $10 cube speaker with “powerful sound,” according to The Verge’s Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, who had a chance to try them out at the show. If one isn’t loud enough, you can pair and sync up to 100 Kallsups to fill a larger space with sound. Battery life is expected to be up to nine hours at half volume on a full charge, and the battery is user-replaceable so you’re not left with e-waste when it stops taking a charge. There’s a long list of gadgets announced at CES 2026 that The Verge’s staff wants, but the Kallsup is the one device we’re probably all going to actually buy. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter Best concept Lenovo Legion Pro Rollable gaming laptop [Media: Lenovo’s ThinkBook Plus Gen 6 was our best in show last year because it was a one-of-a-kind rollable laptop you’d soon be able to own. I really, really hope we’ll be able to soon say the same for Lenovo’s Legion Pro Rollable concept. It takes the rollable OLED formula and extends it horizontally instead of vertically, now attached to a beefy gaming laptop. It’s what I’ve wanted since I saw Lenovo’s first rollable proof of concept back in 2023. What starts out as a conventional 16-inch, 16:10 gaming laptop extends to a 24-inch ultrawide, with a 21.5-inch middle-ground option for good measure. Lenovo didn’t have any games on the laptop for us to test (for shame, Lenovo), but I’ve tested the Legion Pro 7i that the rollable concept is based on, and I liked it enough to give it a nod in our gaming laptop buying guide. Lenovo just needs to make this thing a reality now. If executed well, like in the ThinkBook rollable, this could be the perfect gaming laptop. And it’d be great for multi-monitor-like productivity, too. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer Most “of course they made that” Fraimic Smart Canvas [Image: Have you ever looked at AI art and thought, “Boy oh boy, I wish I could frame that slop right up and stick it on the wall”? Well, you’re in luck. Fraimic is just one of a few companies at CES showing off digital E Ink picture frames designed to display AI-generated art, a concept I’d never considered before this week but which is immediately, painfully obvious in retrospect. Of course someone made this. What makes Fraimic unique in the space is the built-in microphone and voice controls, so you only need talk to the frame to tell it to generate whatever fresh slop your heart desires. It comes in two sizes, priced at either $399 or $999, which includes 100 image generations per year. You can buy more, and the company says it’s considering a $79.99-per-month subscription with unlimited generations — what a bargain. The best thing about Fraimic, and alternatives from the likes of SwitchBot and KoKonna, is that you can ignore the AI element entirely and just display your own pictures and photos instead. At that point you’re looking at a decent-quality E Ink Spectra 6 digital picture frame that doesn’t need to be plugged in and runs for years on a single charge. That we can get behind. — Dominic Preston, news editor Most irrationally loved product LilMilo [Image: “What else can it do?” That was the first question Verge video producer Victoria Barrios had on seeing LilMilo in action, to which the answer is a resounding “nothing.” And yet… don’t you kind of want one anyway? CES has been stuffed to the brim with AI companions and toys this year, and LilMilo — from robot vacuum manufacturer Ecovacs, of all companies — is one of a wave that can only do one thing, and one thing only: sit around and look cute. But look how cute it is! While other companies have opted for cuddly aliens and Totoro-inspired critters, Ecovacs has simply done its best to make a fluffy little pup, and it’s done remarkably well. LilMilo has soft fur and little black toe beans, and thanks to a camera and microphone, it can react to your presence, maintain eye contact, and recognize its owner, supposedly developing its own unique personality over time. I’m more comfortable with AI toys that do this little than I am with the ones that stuff ChatGPT in a teddy bear and hope for the best. But what’s really impressive about LilMilo is that it really does feel strangely alive, an effect only let down by the unsettlingly human eyes. I instinctively gave the little guy the same pets and scritches I usually do my cats, and felt an affection that I know has no rational basis whatsoever. Ecovacs hasn’t confirmed how much LilMilo might cost if and when it launches, and you probably shouldn’t buy one either way — again, it really doesn’t actually do anything. But do you even have to when you look this stinkin’ cute? — Dominic Preston, news editor Most fun MinVerse [Image: I found my favorite thing I’ve ever tried in my four years of attending CES. For me, this year’s CES was a blur of robots that don’t work, vacuums, lawnmowers, and AI chatbots shoved into just about anything. It was a welcome surprise when I stumbled across the booth for Haply, a company that makes haptic controllers for interacting with 3D objects. Haply’s booth showed off a variety of demos, like articulated robot arms that you could control with enough precision to play a real game of Operation, physics demos where you had to push your controller through a gelatinous, spongy 3D object on a screen, and 3D modeling software where you could mold and shape clay. What really surprised me was how much I could feel the objects and their textures through the screen with these controllers, especially its consumer-priced 3D haptics mouse, MinVerse. I used MinVerse briefly in a 3D software application I’ve never used before called Geomagic Freeform and instantly felt comfortable using it because of how tactile the controls were. I’ve dabbled in 3D modeling before as a hobby, but largely gave up on it because typical mice and tablet workflows made the process so cumbersome. 3D sculpting tools were the exact kind of thing I’d always wanted to try but found way too expensive to ever consider, with ranges from $3,000 to $15,000. MinVerse is priced at $1,500, and the company intends to push for further API integration with more affordable programs like Blender, ZBrush, and Maya. While it’s still a hefty cost for a hobbyist, I’m inspired to try 3D modeling again knowing that this tool is out there. — Owen Grove, video director Best sequel Birdbuddy 2 [Image: In between the flashy new TVs, a laptop with a rolling display, and a smartphone that folds in three ways is the Birdbuddy 2. It’s the successor to the smart bird feeder that Birdbuddy launched as part of a Kickstarter campaign in 2020, and now it’s back with a new model that builds upon all the best parts of the Birdbuddy Pro. The Birdbuddy 2 comes with a circular camera housing in the center of the feeder, encapsulating a sensor capable of recording 2K HDR video in a wider 135-degree field of view. The device can capture your feathered visitors in both landscape and portrait mode based on the orientation you choose by physically rotating the camera. It can also record in slow motion, similar to Birdbuddy’s smart hummingbird feeder. The company claims that the Birdbuddy 2 is supposed to start recording as soon as birds land on the feeder. That sounds like a pretty exciting improvement on its own, as I often find myself missing a bird’s initial arrival when reviewing clips from my Birdfy smart feeder. But a better camera isn’t the only upgrade coming to the Birdbuddy 2. The feeder can hold a larger six-cup capacity of bird food and even comes with roof-mounted solar panels, so you don’t have to bring it inside to charge. It’s priced at $199 and is a great upgrade from Birdbuddy’s previous feeders. — Emma Roth, news writer Thing I want to try the most Clicks Power Keyboard [Media: Clicks’ keyboard cases never really appealed to me; as much as I have wanted to mess around with Clicks’ physical keys, I didn’t want to slot my phone into an extra-long case. (My phone is long enough!) But the Clicks Power Keyboard, which puts the keyboard on a magnetic power bank so I can more easily take it on and off my phone? That is something I’m willing to try. The double-duty nature of the device? Super useful. Sliding up my phone to access the keyboard? New fidget toy. The ability to use the keyboard in portrait and landscape mode? Yes please! Bluetooth connectivity, meaning I can use the keyboard even if the bank isn’t attached to my phone? That’s handy. And because it’s a power bank, I can bring it between phones as needed instead of having to buy a whole new bespoke case. Plus, those physical keys look so dang fun. — Jay Peters, senior reporter Best in show Lego Smart Brick [Image: I never would’ve imagined a Lego brick taking home our biggest award at the Consumer Electronics Show, and I say that as a diehard Lego fan. The toymaker hasn’t come to CES for nearly a decade, and we typically give Best in Show to a stunning new screen or chip or a technology that will impact the industry for years. But nothing has captured attention at CES quite like the Lego Smart Brick. My colleagues agree: It’s a breath of fresh air. An AI-free product at a show filled with AI cringe. An idea that seems more compelling when you look deeper, not less. A real product with a real price coming this March, not a concept or prototype. And it was genuinely fun to play with! [Media: When you drop one of these Smart Bricks on a Lego creation, it becomes whatever Lego’s nearby smart NFC tags and figures tell it to become. It can be a spaceship that swoops and soars and refuels and plays a blasting minigame with other ships nearby. It can be a musical instrument that plays certain tunes, a birthday cake whose candles you blow out. It can be a car that accelerates and swerves and crashes and sounds alarms if a bad guy tries to nab it. It can be a Lego creature that purrs when you stroke its back. It can simultaneously roleplay the characters that drive the cars and ships, having them react to a kid’s actions. Kids can mix and match and combine the smarts with normal Lego bricks, repurposing the same lights and sounds and minigames the toymaker has devised for their own creations — powering up any Lego spaceship they build by using the Star Wars X-wing tag, or building a helicopter that quacks like a duck. And it sure sounds like these Smart Bricks won’t just be for kids. The company touts them as its biggest innovation since the minifigure in 1978, and rumor has it that Lego Pokémon will be the next to feature them. — Sean Hollister, senior editor

articles.title: 'Father of iPod' Tony Fadell says that Sam Altman asked 'iPhone designer' Jony Ive to build a physical device for OpenAI as he knows that Apple will never …
articles.summary: Sam Altman asked Jony Ive to build an AI device.
articles.body: ​Sam Altman asked Jony Ive to build an AI device. Tony Fadell, the former Apple executive also known as the “father of the iPod,” says the reason comes down to what Apple lets OpenAI learn from the iPhone. Speaking to*Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon, Fadell said Apple’s privacy restrictions limit the information ChatGPT can gather about a user’s surroundings.​“They have to build products because they cannot get contextual information out of the phone,” Fadell said. He argued that building its own device would let OpenAI use microphones, cameras, GPS and other sensors to give ChatGPT more context. In his view, knowing more about what’s happening around a user could help the assistant answer faster and more accurately.​Why Sam Altman says AI needs a new kind of device​OpenAI pointed Fortune to a video in which Altman gave his own explanation. “The reason we want to do new kinds of consumer hardware is that I think this is a technology that wants a new form factor,” he said. Altman argued that phones and laptops are designed around interfaces people can see and navigate. An AI agent using those same interfaces may have to interpret what’s on the screen to reach information it could otherwise access directly.​Ive, Apple's former design Guru, started working with Altman and OpenAI through his design company LoveFrom. In July 2025, OpenAI announced that io, Ive’s hardware startup, was acquired by the company. Ive and LoveFrom stayed independent and took on design work across OpenAI.​What OpenAI’s device could look like​Fadell said one possibility is a screenless companion device with its own sensors. It could connect over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth and pass information to an AI agent running in the cloud or on a phone. He also pointed to the potential for edge computing, where simpler AI tasks run on a nearby device instead of making a round trip to a remote server.​Fadell floated several forms, including a pendant, a pen and a speaker. Each could collect a different kind of information about what a user is doing or what’s happening nearby. As Fadell put it, “they’re just trying to get context.” ​Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Android’s DIY widgets are a bit of vibe-coding fun
articles.summary: Google’s new Create My Widget tool lets you turn your homescreen into a highly customizable dashboard — but don’t expect too much from it.
articles.body: Aside from dealing with my calendar, there’s one thing I want AI to do: tell me if I’m about to miss the bus. What I need is a widget. It needs to tell me real-time arrivals for the bus stop near my house. Tapping around on my phone screen to open the right app and select my stop will slow me down enough to miss a bus. I need glanceable information, and I hoped that Android’s vibe-coded widget feature could help me out here. It hasn’t, to my disappointment, but I still had a good time cooking up other widgets. Google announced the ability to create custom widgets using AI back at I/O in the spring. It’s called Create My Widget, and it’s part of Android’s suite of “Gemini Intelligence” features. It’s in beta, and only just started rolling out to Pixel phones earlier this month. I was hyped. Not only does this feature raise tantalizing questions like “What is an app?” and “Where does the app live?” — stuff we live for here at The Verge dot com — it has potential to help me make my home screen ridiculous. I fired it up on a Pixel 11 Pro and cooked up my first few widgets, including one that shows a different quote from Jurassic Park every hour — the original film, not any of the sequels, naturally. It took about 20 seconds to make, and it rules. Tapping the widget opens a thread in r/MovieQuotes, so there’s not much software magic going on under the hood, evidently. But did it bring me real joy to read the words “That is one big pile of shit,” on my home screen? It did. I also made a widget that will display the words “Tut tut, looks like rain” whenever it’s raining. This is silly, and it accomplishes nothing except making me happy. I couldn’t think of anything clever it should say when there’s no rain, so it just says “No rain right now” otherwise. But I live in Seattle, so I’ll get a lot of mileage out of this widget. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The create-a-widget interface suggests a few ideas and categories, leaning on more practical uses like habit trackers and recipe inspiration. Fine, I’ll try something normal, I thought. I’m trying to get better about my daily mental health walk, so I had it make a widget for logging a week’s worth of walks. I was hoping for something visual that would trick my little monkey brain into keeping a streak going. Instead, I got something simply labeled “Log Walk” that triggers Gemini to add a walk to my calendar when I tap it. At least Gemini suggested the extra step of creating a checklist where I could mark off the days of the week as I completed my little walk. It took me a minute to get my head around it, but many of the widgets are basically little prompt shortcuts for Gemini. You tap one, it pulls up the Gemini interface on your home screen, thinks for a while, then comes up with whatever you were asking for. The kinds of widgets you can make also seem to fit into some well-defined templates. You can create a widget that displays a countdown to a holiday or certain event on your calendar. You can show a recent score and upcoming game time for your favorite sports team. For anything more open ended, your widget will pull from Google search results (suggest a different three-ingredient cocktail recipe every day, for example) or prompt Gemini to figure it out for you. I was hoping for mini apps I could customize to my liking, but this is more of a one-size-fits-all feature. Fair, I guess. That’s why my bus schedule widget didn’t really work out. I asked for a list of real-time arrivals; it gave me a tile that reads “Bus Arrivals” and uses Gemini to search for arrival times for the stop I specified. Gemini is helpful for some things but useless for this; it gives me a wordy response about how often the bus runs and when I might expect it to arrive based on the schedule. Not what I had in mind. On the bright side, my Jurassic Park quote widget had some words of wisdom for me: “Life, uh, finds a way.” That’ll do for now.

articles.title: The tech products we enthusiastically recommend this holiday season | TechCrunch
articles.summary: We've been reviewing a bunch of new gadgets at TechCrunch this year, and we have some clear favorites to share for your Black Friday shopping and beyond.
articles.body:
We’ve been reviewing a bunch of new gadgets and hardware at TechCrunch this year: dumb phones , bird feeders , health trackers , slushy machines , AI mattress pads , you name it. Sometimes we think they’re unnecessary and expensive , but other times, we try out devices that we love so much that we go out and buy them ourselves.

If these products can impress a group of (sometimes) curmudgeonly tech reporters, then they’re sure to please whoever you’re shopping for this holiday season.

We’ve updated this article with new Black Friday pricing for some of our recommendations. Black Friday deals are likely to end by the end of November 30 (Cyber Monday).

We’ve reviewed a lot of e-readers this year. What can we say? We’re nerds. We work for a tech website. But after trying devices from the usual suspects as well as some wildcards, we have recommendations. Evidently, 2026 was the year we fell in love with the pocket-sized e-reader.

Xteink X3 ($55) — a budget pick for someone techy

It’s an e-reader so small that it can fit in your wallet, or even magnetize to the back of your phone. Do you dream of a world where instead of scrolling Instagram when you’re waiting in line for coffee, you actually opt to read books? There’s really something special about the Xteink X3 , and it’s only $55 during Xteink’s Black Friday sale . Fair warning, it takes some fiddling with to set up, and it has no integration with Kindle, Libby, or any other apps, so only buy this for someone willing to do a bit of Reddit browsing and tinkering to get it up and running.

Xteink X4 Pro ($84) — it has a backlight!

If you aren’t planning to magnetize the Xteink to your phone, you’ve got to go with the X4 Pro , which is also discounted for Black Friday . It’s slightly bigger, but it has a backlight, which makes it way more versatile. After using both the X3 and the X4 Pro , I find that the backlight really is a game changer, since I do a lot of reading in bed — plus, I like my Pop Socket wallet a bit too much to displace it for the X3, and I’d rather just carry an extra credit card-sized device than risk forgetting my actual credit and ID cards, which I have grown too used to having on my phone.

Boox Palma Pro 2 ($400) — a phone-sized e-reader without the drawbacks

If I’m being honest, reading my colleague Aisha Malik’s review of the Boox Palma Pro 2 is making me want to buy one. I love using the Xteink e-readers, but they don’t connect to any outside apps. As a hardcore Libby power user (a phrase I am saying in earnest sincerity), it’s a bit frustrating that I can’t get my library books on Xteink e-readers. The same goes for apps like Kobo and Kindle, where any e-book you already own cannot be transferred out of the Amazon ecosystem unless the publisher agrees, which most do not.

If you’re looking for an e-reader with a screen that’s actually book-sized, my favorite that I’ve used is the Kobo Libra Colour , which is $259. The Amazon Paperwhite line is great, but c’mon, Amazon. Branch out!

Hey, we’ve all got to eat. And if you want, you can make that eating process overly techy. Why not?

Ember Mug 3 ($99) — for the tea lover who’s really particular

The Ember Mug 3 is the latest iteration in Ember’s line of coffee/tea cups that actually stay warm. Our reviewer Lauren Forristal especially appreciated that you no longer need to use your phone app to change the mug’s temperature, which seems like it would be really annoying!

This mug is perfect for gifting to someone, or to put on your own wish list — you might not want to spend $99 (or $94 right now for Black Friday ) on a mug for yourself, but these sorts of luxury, nice-to-haves are what holidays are made for!

Ninja Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer ($449.99) — two appliances in one!

Ah, Ninja, the premiere company in the business of turning every appliance into a two-in-one air fryer. I jest, but at least Ninja knows it’s on to something. Despite the Ninja Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer ‘s high price point, Lauren says that this new product made “a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one.” You can’t buy more counter space (without moving), but you can buy more versatile appliances. There’s a $100 off Black Friday deal here .

GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro ($499.99) — if your fridge has a built-in ice maker, you just won’t understand

Sure, there are cheaper ice makers on the market. But Aisha clarifies that this is the ice maker for “those who crave what’s called ‘the good ice.’” If you feel so passionately about the ice in your beverages that you know what she means, then maybe this is for you. Right now it’s reduced to $349.99 in Amazon’s Black Friday sale .

What they really want is a Mac mini or Claude subscription, but if that’s out of budget, we have some other ideas that might impress your AI-pilled, vibe-coder loved ones …

Open AI Codex Micro ($230) — for the Codex evangelist

When I asked my colleague Lucas Ropek what about his favorite product he reviewed this year, he mentioned the Codex Micro . Some hard-core coders — who the product is aimed toward — have found this thing less than pleasing, but Lucas seems to have had fun figuring out this first attempt by OpenAI at hardware.

Best case, it’s a productivity game-changer for your friend who has a hardworking team of AI agents within the OpenAI ecosystem. Worst case, this will be a great piece of tech history in a few years.

For the person who’s desperate to log off

As people have become more conscious about how much time they spend online, new tech has emerged that, ironically, is designed to keep you away from tech. Some of these products can really make a difference in your life.

Brick ($59) or Brick Night ($129) — a not-so-subtle gift for your friend who doomscrolls every night before bed

For about six months, I’ve consistently used the Brick to prevent me from using social media as the last thing I do before bed, or the first thing in the morning. Some people use it to help them focus during the workday, but evidently, I was not the only one who needed Brick’s help with sleep. The company recently launched its second device, Brick Night , which “Bricks” your phone when you are in the same room. You can customize the times that the Brick Night is active, so it’s not as though you can never, ever use social media in your room. Both Brick and Brick Night are very customizable, so you can create the perfect setup tailored to your needs.

It’s embarrassing how wholeheartedly I recommend the Brick, which is basically just a hunk of plastic with an NFC chip in it and a companion app. But my sleep has improved significantly — I even do 8 a.m. Pilates now. Who am I?

Brick has a small discount to $56.80 for Black Friday on Amazon .

Dumb Phone ($20 + service plan) — for someone who wants to try something new but can’t totally give up their iPhone

I’ve tried out far pricier smart phone alternatives, but the Dumb Phone was both the most affordable, and the most usable for me. In the humble shell of a $20 TCL flip phone , Dumb Co loads its own software so that users can access apps like WhatsApp, Spotify, Apple Music, and Uber. You can even access iMessage through a third-party app, though Apple could probably get that shut down … no one tell Apple, please!

The Dumb Phone is particularly usable because it’s not intended to be a complete replacement for your smartphone — it’s more like a companion device that you can take out with you when you want to feel more present in the world but still may need to call an Uber home.

Wearable health trackers are pretty common nowadays, but after reviewing several different rings and wristbands , Aisha has named a winner.

There are a lot of ugly health trackers. And then there’s the Oura Ring 5 , the leading smart ring maker’s first product that’s thin enough to wear without loudly broadcasting to the world that you’re monitoring your heart rate. (For what it’s worth, I tried the RingConn 3 — which is about the same size as Oura Ring 5 — but returned it, unsatisfied. Womp womp.) Aisha notes in her review that the newest Oura Ring 5 is more durable, has a better battery life, and looks more premium than its predecessors. It’s also part of Amazon’s Black Friday sale, now priced starting at $299 .

This post originally published November 15 and has since been updated to reflect new promotional pricing.

articles.summary: 'Shayad Yahi Hai Pyaar' has been exploring the many shades of falling in love.
articles.body: 'Shayad Yahi Hai Pyaar' has been exploring the many shades of falling in love. The show has been striking a chord with audiences for its refreshing and emotionally nuanced take on a relationship. Starring Aditi Dev Sharma as Preeti and Daksh Puri as Aarav, the show, an Indian adaptation of the popular Korean drama ‘Something in the Rain’, has made many wonder if love can transcend age. And just when Preeti and Aarav seem to be finding their footing together, their love story is about to encounter another universal relationship hurdle – jealousy.Adding a fresh twist to the narrative is international model and actor Irina Rudakova, who makes her fiction comeback as Zoe, Aarav's former girlfriend from the USA. Confident, glamorous and clear about what she wants, Zoe returns with feelings that are far from resolved. She confides in Preeti that she wants to rekindle her relationship with Aarav and is even considering proposing to him to see if they can give their romance another chance. Her candid revelation leaves Preeti rattled. She begins doubting her place in his life as she is faced with someone who is younger, attractive and shares a romantic history with Aarav.Talking about her return to fiction and joining ‘Shayad Yahi Hai Pyaar’, Irina Rudakova shares, "India has given me so much love over the years, and now getting to tell a love story here feels like everything has come full circle. I am genuinely happy to be back in the fiction arena after exploring different reality formats for quite some time. Having travelled across different parts of the world, I've seen the universal appeal of love as an emotion, but the way it is experienced, expressed and understood in India is very distinct culturally coded. That is something I find particularly beautiful about India. There is an intensity, warmth and emotional depth to relationships here that makes even the simplest moments feel meaningful. And so I am delighted to be strengthening my bond with Indian audiences through this show and hope they enjoy discovering Zoe as much as I have enjoyed bringing her to life."Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. articles.title: You might lose your Oura health data if you’re still using an old Android phone
articles.summary: Oura is ending app support for Android 11 on December 8th, and users who don’t upgrade before then will lose ‘historical’ data.
articles.body: Oura will be dropping support for Android 11 on December 8th, 2026, and users may not have access to all of their data if they don’t upgrade to Android 12 or higher before the deadline. The support page now reads: > Oura will drop support for Android 11 on December 8, 2026. If you are using an Android device, be sure to update to Android 12 or higher to ensure no loss of data or features. If you decide not to upgrade, you may still be able to use some limited historical Oura App features. Please note that if you do upgrade your smartphone system later, your historical Oura data will not carry over. Companies often end support for older OSes, and Android 11 came out in 2020, so it’s getting a bit long in the tooth. Normally, though, this just means missing out on new features or bug fixes. Losing historical health data is more surprising, and Oura offers no explanation for why the data wouldn’t be preserved. If you’ve been procrastinating updating your phone, or hemming and hawing about replacing it, now might be the time to finally take the plunge. If you’re not quite ready to, at least make sure to head to the membership hub and export your data so you have a backup ahead of December 8th.

articles.title: My favorite MPC beat maker is ready for your vibe-coded firmware and effects
articles.summary: The Akai MPC Sample 1.4 firmware officially opens up the device to modders and third-party developers through an SDK and custom effects plugins.
articles.body: Akai is continuing to open up its various music-making platforms with the MPC Sample 1.4 firmware. My favorite (and the most affordable) of the MPC samplers has become a popular home for vibe-coded custom firmwares and mods. The company has decided, rather than fight it, to embrace the modding community. The latest update adds several new developer features, including support for the new SDK and custom Knob Effects plugins. Plugins added to the appropriate folder on your microSD card are now automatically recognized and will appear at the bottom of the list in the Knob Effects menu. There’s also a Developer Mode, which lets you run scripts from the microSD card or access the sampler’s internal filesystem over USB, which will be handy for all those modders vibe-coding their own add-ons for the MPC. There’s also remote screen access for mirroring the display on an external monitor through the MPC Remote Screen Viewer app. [Media: There are a few other nice updates, including flatten pad, which speeds up the resampling process for baking in effects on individual pads, and sequence record autoplay, which adds a looper-like experience. Akai also added a scale option to the 16-levels pad mode, so you’re not limited to 16 chromatic notes, and can instead play melodic one-shots in E minor pentatonic, B major, or whatever key your track happens to be in. articles.title: Allstate has been suffering an outage since Monday
articles.summary: Allstate, one of the country’s largest insurance companies, has been dealing with a major outage for five days.
articles.body: On Monday, November 23rd, Allstate began dealing with an outage that has impacted its website, mobile apps, and roadside assistance service. It’s just the latest company, including Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase, to suffer an outage in the last few weeks. As of Friday afternoon, access to accounts through the app and site appeared to still be down. When asked for comment, the company pointed us to a notice on its site reading: > Allstate customers can reach us in many ways, including online, by phone and through local offices. Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims. To the extent service interruptions impact a customer’s ability to make a payment, they won’t lose coverage or be charged late fees. Opening the app pops up a notification saying the company is working to “restore access as soon as possible,” and encourages customers to contact the company by phone to file and manage claims. Users have flooded X and Reddit with complaints about the outage, some of whom have either been left waiting for roadside assistance or have been unable to insure new vehicles. Allstate hasn’t publicly identified a cause for the outage.

articles.title: The new iPad Mini is getting its first major discount for Black Friday
articles.summary: Apple’s latest iPad Mini is $100 off at multiple retailers for Black Friday, dropping the 128GB Wi-Fi configuration with an 8.5-inch OLED display to a cool $599.
articles.body: We were big fans of Apple’s new iPad Mini when we reviewed it in early November, but its steep starting price of $699 was hard to swallow. Thankfully, the small tablet is already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. Right now, Amazon and Walmart are both selling the 2026 iPad Mini with Wi-Fi and 128GB of storage starting at $599 ($100 off), its lowest price to date. [Product: iPad Mini (2026) | The new Mini is a notable upgrade over its predecessor, with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display that delivers deeper blacks and better contrast than the previous model’s 8.3-inch LCD. Despite the bigger screen, the tablet itself is smaller and lighter, making it easier to carry. Apple also added IP67 dust and water resistance, so you have less reason to worry about where you use it. As my colleague David Pierce noted in his review, that made a big difference in his day-to-day use; he felt more comfortable handing the Mini to his spill-prone toddler or keeping it nearby in the kitchen to follow recipes. He even took it into the shower to keep watching a football game. The upgraded A20 Pro chip also made apps load faster and demanding games run better in Pierce’s testing, while battery life held steady at around nine hours of screentime. At $599, though, the new Mini is still relatively expensive if you mainly want a tablet for browsing the web or streaming shows. The last-gen iPad Mini, which runs on Apple’s A17 Pro chip, is available for under $500 if you’d rather save another $100 and can live without the OLED screen and water resistance. But if you’ve been waiting for a more worthwhile upgrade to Apple’s smallest tablet, the current Black Friday discount makes the new model easier to justify. articles.title: This purple electric Chinese minivan can go up to 559 miles on a charge
articles.summary: The BYD Whale electric minivan has been announced at the Guangzhou Auto Show, with 900km of battery range.
articles.body: Electric minivans could be the ultimate in utility, with room for passengers, gear, and huge batteries. While VW’s ID Buzz only gave us 200 miles of real-world driving on a charge in 2023, China’s BYD has just announced a flagship purple peoplemover that can go an estimated 559 miles (900 km) on electricity. It’s called the BYD Whale, and some back-of-the-napkin math suggests it lives up to the name. The van would be bigger than a Honda Odyssey, bigger than a Chrysler Pacifica, and bigger than a Toyota Sienna, at 17.3 feet (5,270mm) long, 6.5 feet (1,996mm) wide, 6 feet (1,815mm) tall, and with a 123-inch (3,130mm) wheelbase. [Image: [Image: According to an auto-translated press release, the vehicle should have room for seven passengers and seven suitcases at a time, not that the company has shown off its interior yet. You can see a prominent sensor cluster on its forehead, though, and it’ll come equipped with LiDAR for advanced hands-free driving. [Image: [Image: CarNewsChina points out it’s actually not the first with 900 km of CLTC battery range on board — Geely’s all electric Zeekr 009 minivan also claims to offer up to 900 km of range in one configuration. But BYD’s also claiming the can charge its battery from 10 percent to 97 percent in just nine minutes, and it get you from 10 percent to 70 percent in five minutes, according to Electrek. The Whale will also come in a 248-mile (400 km) plug-in hybrid version as well, and the company’s planning to ship it in China in Q1 of 2027 for around 300,000 yuan. That’s roughly $45,000. As we’ve reported, Chinese cars are becoming quite competitive. Will they make it to the US?

articles.title: Sony’s 1000XM4C headphones are a Black Friday bargain at $198
articles.summary: Sony revised its classic WH-1000XM4 noise canceling headphones with improved specs, and they’re $100 off during Black Friday.
articles.body: Instead of purely looking forward with its headphone designs, Sony went back to its popular WH-1000XM4 design and made some improvements to make it even better. The 2026 version, called the WH-1000XM4C, sounds nearly as good as the pricier XM6 model (currently $348), but is down to $198 during Black Friday at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart. That’s $100 off their October launch price. [Product: Sony WH-1000XM4C | There’s a reason why Sony went back to refine the XM4. Our former reviewer Chris Welch praised them for being super comfortable and for having close to perfect features for the price, especially compared to its successor, the XM3 (still my daily driver, for what it’s worth). The XM4s had better sound quality and noise cancellation, plus improved mics, multipoint connectivity, and a sensor that can detect when you remove them to automatically pause audio. Now, with the XM4C, there are further improvements, most notably a 10-band equalizer in the app (compared to the original XM4’s five-band) that my colleague John Higgins says really helped the headphones’ midrange frequencies open up. These are a great buy, but they aren’t your only Sony headphones deal to consider right now. Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are available during Black Friday at Best Buy for $169, their lowest price yet from a major retailer. There are upsides and downsides to this model: They feature improved noise cancellation thanks to more mics, despite using the same ANC chip as the XM4C, but they can’t fold up as compactly, making them a little bigger to pack in your bag. Either one you choose, you’ll have some great headphones to listen to going into 2027. Read our Sony WH-1000XM4C review.
